dispositions.reason: Documented: Borromeo's own letter and the first provincial council's seminary decree cite Trent's command.

dispositions.reason: Same link. 'One ordinary parish' is loose (he reshaped a province), but the paragraph scores below the reading target and a one-word fix would force a full rewrite, so it is flagged for the reviewer rather than changed.

dispositions.reason: Inferential-Thin: Giussano names the rite Milan always kept and Borromeo's guarding of it; its descent from Ambrose's own day is not shown. Wording kept in prose change 2.

dispositions.reason: A fact about his cult, not a tie to another movement. Kept, in plainer words.

links.note: Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus by bull in 1540. In 1546 Ignatius sent instructions to his men at the Council of Trent, where Laínez and Salmerón served as the pope's theologians. Laínez argued there against a two-part view of justification, and the council's decree ruled it out.
links.outcome_considered: The decree on justification is the council's own teaching, and no listed source shows it adopted because of the Jesuits; Waterworth says only that Laínez argued ably and the decree aimed at Seripando's view. No institutional act results from the relationship itself.

links.note: Borromeo's biographer says Milan had always kept the Ambrosian rite. Borromeo revised its Missal and let no one depart from it, because it was so old. Augustine says Ambrose's church began singing hymns in 386. How much of the later rite goes back to Ambrose is unclear.
links.outcome_considered: Borromeo's revision of the Ambrosian Missal is Milan's own liturgical act; it keeps an inherited rite rather than resulting from any act of Ambrose's Milan, and the descent of the rite from Ambrose's day is itself uncertain.

links.note: In 1570 Pope Pius V issued the Roman Missal, reformed under a decree of the Council of Trent. It stayed the standard Mass book until the Second Vatican Council's liturgy decree of 1963 ordered the rite revised. That later decree is cited here by name only, so this tie is thin.

prose_changes.old: Spearhead of Catholic reform; parent of the mission-born traditions
prose_changes.new: A driving force of Catholic reform. Its theologians spoke at the Council of Trent, and its missions began the churches of Japan and China.
prose_changes.reason: 'Parent of the mission-born traditions' overclaims: the Kongo church began with the Portuguese mission of 1491, before the Society existed, and the first missions in New Spain were not Jesuit. The Jesuit origin is documented for Japan (Xavier, 1549) and China (Trigault, 1583), so the sentence names those two. 'Spearhead' becomes 'a driving force', carried by the Widely Accepted link to the Tridentine Church; the jes world rates the founding as a response to the Reformation Contested, so the text claims reform, not reaction.

prose_changes.old: The Society still exists and is the largest religious order of men in the Catholic Church; in 2013 one of its members became the first Jesuit pope. Its lasting institutional bequest is education — a worldwide network of schools and universities. And its lasting spiritual one is the Spiritual Exercises, still made as eight-day and thirty-day retreats by Catholics and, increasingly, by Protestants. Its missionaries' letters home also gave Europe some of its first sustained descriptions of Japan, China and the Americas.
prose_changes.new: The Society still exists. It is the largest order of men in the Catholic Church, and in 2013 one of its members became the first Jesuit pope. Its great gift to the world of learning is a worldwide network of schools and universities. Its great spiritual gift is the Spiritual Exercises, still made today as retreats of eight or thirty days. Its missionaries' letters home also gave Europe some of its first long accounts of Japan, China and the Americas.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source shows Protestants making the Exercises, or a growing number of them; 'and, increasingly, by Protestants' is removed, and 'by Catholics' with it. The old paragraph scored below the reading target, so the rest is split into shorter sentences with the same facts.

prose_changes.old: Borromeo's Milan became the template. His Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis, published in 1582, circulated as a working handbook for bishops across the Catholic world, and the parish shape it describes — a trained resident priest, regular catechism, the confessional, the visitation — lasted into the twentieth century. Charles Borromeo remains one of Catholicism's most widely invoked patrons of bishops and seminarians, and his diocese still keeps the Ambrosian rite that long predates him.
prose_changes.new: Borromeo's Milan became a model. His book of rules for Milan, the Acta Ecclesiae Mediolanensis, first came out in 1582. It gathered the decrees of his councils, and bishops in many lands used it as a working handbook. The parish it describes lasted into the twentieth century. It had a trained priest who lived among his people, regular lessons in the faith, the confessional and the bishop's visit. Catholics still call on Charles Borromeo as patron of bishops and of men training to be priests. His diocese still keeps the Ambrosian rite, which is far older than he is.
prose_changes.reason: 'Became the template' and 'circulated ... for bishops across the Catholic world' are wider than the evidence. Peña (1610) says bishops in many provinces and kingdoms followed his example and his councils' decrees; the text now says 'a model' and 'bishops in many lands', carried by the Widely Accepted link to the Tridentine Church. The Ambrosian clause is kept and carried by the Inferential-Thin link from Ambrosian Milan. The old paragraph scored far below the reading target, so it is split into shorter sentences with the same facts.

prose_changes.old: Teresa of Ávila had spent more than twenty years as a Carmelite nun in a large, comfortable, sociable convent when she concluded that the life she had promised was not the life she was living. In 1562 she founded a small house, St Joseph's in Ávila, under a stricter rule — poverty, enclosure, few sisters, long hours of silent prayer. And spent the rest of her life traveling Spain founding others, arguing with officials, and writing books about prayer she had never intended to publish. In 1568 a young friar, John of the Cross, joined the reform on the men's side and became its greatest poet. Both were watched by the Inquisition and opposed from inside their own order, and John spent nine months imprisoned by his own brethren. Which is when he wrote some of his finest verse.
prose_changes.new: Teresa of Ávila had spent more than twenty years as a Carmelite nun in a large, comfortable, sociable convent when she concluded that the life she had promised was not the life she was living. In 1562 she founded a small house, St Joseph's in Ávila, under a stricter rule — poverty, enclosure, few sisters, long hours of silent prayer. And spent the rest of her life traveling Spain founding others, arguing with officials, and writing books about prayer she had never intended to publish. In 1568 a young friar, John of the Cross, joined the reform on the men's side and became its greatest poet. The Inquisition examined Teresa's account of her life, and both were opposed from inside their own order. John spent nine months imprisoned by his own brethren. Which is when he wrote some of his finest verse.
prose_changes.reason: The Inquisition's examination of Teresa's Life is shown (Zimmerman's introduction to the 1904 Life, lines 2154-2161: the Princess of Eboli denounced it in 1574 and the Inquisition named censors). No vendored text shows the Inquisition watching John in his lifetime, so the claim is narrowed to Teresa. 'Nine months' is kept: the 1873 Life says 'more than eight months' (line 4586), December 1577 to August 1578, and nine is the usual round figure. One sentence changed.

prose_changes.old: The Discalced Carmelites are still a worldwide order of friars and nuns. Teresa's and John's writings became permanent classics of Christian spiritual literature far beyond Catholicism, read by Protestants, by poets and by psychologists, and both were later declared Doctors of the Church — Teresa in 1970, the first woman ever so named. Their vocabulary passed into ordinary English: the 'dark night of the soul', the 'interior castle'.
prose_changes.new: The Discalced Carmelites are still a worldwide order of friars and nuns. Teresa's and John's writings became lasting classics of Christian prayer, translated and read far beyond Spain. Both were later named Doctors of the Church. Teresa, named in 1970, was the first woman to hold that title. Their words passed into ordinary English: the 'dark night of the soul', the 'interior castle'.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source shows their reading by Protestants, poets or psychologists, or 'far beyond Catholicism'. The vendored English translations (Lewis 1891-1913, Stanbrook 1912-19) show them translated and read far beyond Spain, which is what the text now says. The old paragraph scored below the reading target, so the long sentence is split.
